newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: PM PROMISES HELP FOR BHP STAFF

The Prime Minister says he's deeply concerned about the psychological effect the closure of BHP's steelworks at Newcastle will have on the region and other parts of Australia. BHP says it will close its steel plant within two years, and shut down operations in Sydney, Melbourne and Geelong.
Mr Howard says the government can't intervene to reverse a commercial decision, but will do what it can to help those affected by the closure, within the bounds of realism.
HOWARD DISMISSES CLAIMS 1 IN 4 WOULD VOTE FOR HANSON
The Prime Minister says he expects electoral support for Independent MP Pauline Hanson will dry up when it's realised she doesn't have any superior answers.
John Howard's rejected claims Ms Hanson's and her One Nation party could pose a threat at the next election.
That's despite the Queensland Premier's warning that her support could strengthen into a right-wing revolt.
Mr Howard has told radio 3AW in Melbourne that some voters may be feeling uneasy or insecure, and says a poll showing 10 per cent of voters support Pauline Hanson isn't surprising.
He dismissed as nonsense, other polls showing 25 per cent of voters would consider voting for her party.
WARNING HANSON COULD SPARK RECESSION
A former Northern Territory Chief Minister, Paul Everingham, says senior business people and politicians in Malaysia have told him Pauline Hanson is a real threat to trade with Australia.
Mr Everingham, who's now the Honorary Malaysia Consul for Queensland, says a poll showing Ms Hanson has 20 per cent support in Queensland, makes this issue more serious than native title.
Mr Everingham says he's frightened that Ms Hanson and her One Nation Party will spark a recession.
He says Australia's ability to create jobs depends on its ability to trade with Asian countries and get investment from them.
CLAIMS OF DELIBERATE STALLING ON CENTURY ZINC MINE
ATSIC says the start of the billion-dollar Century Zinc mine is being deliberately delayed until the Prime Minister announces the Government's response to the Wik decision.
ATSIC deputy, Ray Robinson, says after securing the approval of the remaining native title claimants, he should have received some sort of response from the State or the mining company.
Mr Robinson says says mining companies, graziers and the media have been using the Wik decision to push a perception that Aborigines can't negotiate.
He says the stalling of the mine is a ploy by the Queensland Premier and Century Zinc who don't want to admit that Aboriginal people can and are negotiating on native title.
AUSTRALIA SUFFERING FROM "WINNER TAKES ALL" ATTITUDE-ACOSS
The president of Australia's peak welfare organisation says Australia is in the grip of a new "winner takes all" attitude.
Robert Fitzgerald from the Australian Council of Social Service says there's been a shift in national values, with a lessening of regard and concern for people.
Speaking at a conference examining social policy changes in Canberra, Mr Fitzgerald says the tolerance of an unemployment rate of more than eight per cent is an example of the shift.
He says no longer are the unemployed regarded as being one of the most disadvantaged in our community, and gone is the belief that everyone has a right and entitlement to work.
OPTUS DEFENDING CABLES AFTER AUSTEL RULING
Pay TV company Optus is again defending its overhead cables, following a successful bid by a northern Sydney resident to have cables removed from outside her house.
Optus has pulled cables back from the the front of artist, Josonia Palaitis's home, following her complaint to industry watchdog Austel that they reduced her home's value.
The company's Glen Thomas says the position of Ms Palaitis' house enabled Optus to re-route the cables.
But he told ABC Radio, Ms Palaitis' was unique, and Optus won't be responding to every resident's objection.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
